1:
The one new word in the title, destroy not, is explained five ways. Adam Clarke reconstructs a scene: when Saul was providentially delivered into David’s hand in the cave, David may have formed the hasty resolution to take his life, as his companions counselled, and in that moment received the divine monition — destroy not, lift not up thy hand against the Lord’s anointed — so that afterwards, composing the psalm, he gave it for a title the words of the warning. Matthew Henry allows that sense but prefers the reverse: God would not let David be destroyed by Saul, permitting the persecution only under that limitation, as he permitted Satan to afflict Job with the proviso that his life be saved. John Calvin says we are left entirely to conjecture and lists three — the opening of a song well known at the time, an expression uttered by David in his extremity, or a commendation of the principle he showed in preventing Abishai from slaying Saul. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the words refer to any such incident: this is a direction for musical execution, to be sung to that melody, and the Geneva version renders it correctly. Augustine of Hippo works from a different title altogether, taking the words at the end for Christ, who is called the end not as one that consumes but as one that consummates, and reads the psalm of the Passion.

Which cave is also unsettled. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the inscription says only that he fled from Saul in the cave, and that the connection in the history from which the statement was extracted would have shown whether it belongs to the cave of Adullam or the labyrinthine cave on the heights of Engedi by the sheep-folds — for which they send the reader to a modern traveller’s journal. Adam Clarke settles on Engedi without hesitation. On the doubled plea for mercy C.H. Spurgeon says that he who would receive quickly must ask twice, and that faith, though it does not deserve mercy, always wins it. John Gill reads the repetition as a mark of the greatness of the distress and the vehemence of the prayer. Charles Ellicott would render trusteth as has taken refuge, and the calamities as the danger of destruction, which he thinks gives the feeling of the Hebrew better.

What comes from heaven divides the entry again. John Gill reports the Targum supplying his angel and Kimchi his angels, the ministering spirits who encamped about Jacob and released Peter, but prefers the sense that David looked for no help from men on earth and expected it from above, with a possible further view to the mission of Christ. Adam Clarke allows both, that God would send his angels were there no earthly agents, or that he will give the command from heaven for it to be done on earth; and he personifies the next clause, making mercy and truth themselves the messengers, mercy inclining God to save and truth binding him to fulfil what mercy has promised. John Wesley keeps it to the promises being made good. Charles Ellicott attends to the mechanics: the pause-word stands in the middle of the verse as awkwardly as elsewhere, and the Greek places it after the previous verse; the marginal correction of the second clause is decidedly to be adopted, the word given as reproach being used in the sense of rebuke. Adam Clarke had reached the same conclusion about the pause-word by feel, saying simply that he thinks it should stand at the end of the verse. On the clause about God performing all things Charles Ellicott notes that the Greek and Latin read one letter differently and give my benefactor, an emendation he would adopt, while Adam Clarke keeps the received word as one who completes for me and will bring all to a happy issue.
4:
Whether the soul is among lions is the first question. Adam Clarke sides with Dr Kennicott against the received text and would read that his soul dwells in parched places, from a root meaning to thirst, which he thinks the Chaldee also understood; the next clause he takes to mean that he seems to be among coals. John Gill keeps the lions as a figure for men stout, fierce and cruel, and is careful whom he means: not David’s own men, as some think, who would gladly have killed Saul in the cave, but Saul and the three thousand chosen men with him. He notes that Scripture regularly names persecuting princes lions, and that Homer compares Achilles to one for his cruelty. Charles Ellicott corrects the second phrase to greedy ones, literally lickers, in apposition to the lions, and reads the verse as the plain insecurity of a man whose dwelling is among foes and who must sleep every night with danger all round him — from which situation, he adds, the refrain that follows rises grandly. John Wesley makes them firebrands set on fire from hell, breathing out wrath and incensing Saul.

On the refrain John Gill takes the exaltation as a request that God show himself God by saving him and disappointing his enemies, and John Wesley as a request that power, goodness, justice and faithfulness be glorified to the highest degree possible; Adam Clarke reports that several of the fathers apply the verse before to the passion of the Lord and this one to his resurrection. On the net and the pit Adam Clarke explains the apparatus — a springe set where the prey is known to pass, and a pit covered with weak sticks and turf so that the beast falls through — and turns it on Saul, who dug pits for David and fell into one himself at the cave, walking into the very place where David lay hidden.

Adam Clarke then reports a rabbinic tale: God sent a spider to weave her web across the mouth of the cave, so that Saul, seeing it, naturally concluded the place was the haunt of neither men nor beasts and went in to rest. It may be a fable, Clarke allows, but it shows by what apparently insignificant means the universal ruler can accomplish the greatest ends; and he collects three proverbs to the same effect, the English one that harm watch is harm catch, a Greek saying that evil advice is most ruinous to the adviser, and a Latin couplet holding no law juster than that which makes the inventor of an instrument of death die by it. Charles Ellicott finds the verse damaged rather than pointed. The verb rendered as the soul being bowed down is everywhere else transitive, and the Greek and Latin accordingly have that they pressed down his soul; Ewald alters my soul to their soul in defiance of the grammar; but no conjecture of the kind restores the parallelism, which he judges here hopelessly lost, since what we expect is that they prepared a net and were caught in it themselves. John Gill is content that the snares were the insidious ways used to get David into their hands, as the Pharisees consulted how to entangle Christ in his talk.
7:
C.H. Spurgeon notes what the psalmist does not say: one would have expected my heart is fluttered, and instead it is fixed, twice over — when the central axle is secure the whole wheel is right, and if the great anchor holds the ship cannot drive. He has the singer resolving that neither Satan nor Saul shall stop him, and that he will make the cavern ring with music. Matthew Henry marks how strangely the tune is altered, the complaints turned all at once into thanksgiving, and reads the fixed heart as one lifted up which had been bowed down before, prepared for every event because stayed upon God. John Gill takes the fixedness for assurance of salvation and adds the alternative rendering, that the heart is prepared or ready to receive good or evil at God’s hand. Adam Clarke makes it a firm purpose to do and suffer God’s will, and John Wesley a steadfast belief of the promises.

What it is that must awake divides the entry. John Gill takes the glory for the soul, which the patriarch called his honour, and explains how a soul can be asleep — not literally, being incorporeal, but when grace is dormant, when it is slothful in duty and lukewarm through prevailing corruptions and worldly cares, or dulled and pressed down by sorrow. Adam Clarke takes the clause out of the soul altogether: one manuscript and the Syriac read my harp rather than my glory, and Dr Kennicott a word he supposes to be some instrument of music, noting that the instrument used in Ethiopian church music bears a like name. Clarke thinks the Syriac reading the true one — awake up, my harp; awake, psaltery and harp — such repetitions being frequent in the Hebrew poets; and if the received word stands, he refers it to the tongue or, more likely, to the psalmist’s own skill in composition and playing. John Wesley takes it simply for the tongue, and C.H. Spurgeon for the noblest powers together, the intellect that conceives the thought, the tongue that expresses it and the imagination that beautifies it. Charles Ellicott shifts the waking to the other party: rather than the singer waking early, he would have him rouse the dawn, and cites the poet in whom the cock calls forth the morning and, still nearer, the English lines about hounds and horn cheerily rousing the slumbering morn.

Adam Clarke presses the harp further than anyone. A rabbinic tradition holds that David had a harp at his bed’s head which played of itself when the north wind blew on it, whereupon he rose to praise God; grave Christian writers have treated this as a ridiculous fable, but Clarke hesitates and asks whether the account does not point to an instrument then well known and answering to the one lately rediscovered that is sounded by the wind. He also observes that the last five verses of this psalm are nearly the same as the opening of another, and suggests that notes from the psalmist’s diary were probably copied twice by mistake, since the insertion at the head of that other psalm seems to bear no relation to the rest of the ode. On the praise among the nations John Gill hesitates between the tribes of Israel meeting together and the Gentiles, while Adam Clarke takes it for a prophecy that these compositions should be sung in synagogues and in Christian churches everywhere — and so it is, he says, for wherever the name of Christ is known, David’s is known also. John Gill traces the mercy that reaches the heavens from the heart of God through the covenant to pardon and eternal life, and Adam Clarke ends by observing that David is here not merely happy but in a state of triumph, encompassed by ferocious enemies with everything against him except God and his innocence.
